1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Vision-language-action models (VLAs) fine-tune pretrained language models on robot demonstrations to produce actions from visual observations and language instructions~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla}, but which of the resulting representational changes reflect action training and which are inherited from the pretrained backbone?
5	In these decoder-only architectures, image tokens precede instruction tokens, and the causal attention mask restricts multimodal integration to a single readout token~\cite{wang2025seeing,pei2025rethinking}; how representations at this critical position are reshaped by action fine-tuning remains unknown.
6	
7	Behavioral studies show that VLAs exhibit visual dominance~\cite{grant2026} and underweight instructions~\cite{haon2025}, but existing representational analyses target single architectures.
8	No prior work tests whether instruction routing---the internal mechanisms by which instruction tokens influence action-relevant representations---is consistent across backbone families or decomposes training-associated effects from inherited base-model priors.
9	
10	We address this gap with a cross-architecture analysis of three VLAs (OpenVLA~\cite{kim2024_openvla}, TraceVLA~\cite{zheng2024tracevla}, and NORA~\cite{hung2025nora}) across four LIBERO~\cite{liu2023_libero} task suites (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
11	TraceVLA and NORA baselines are pure VLMs ($N = 2$ independent VLM-to-VLA transitions); OpenVLA's baseline is the OXE-pretrained~\cite{padalkar2023_oxe} VLA (VLA-to-VLA transition).

2	
3	\paragraph{Vision-language-action models.}
4	VLAs fine-tune large language models on robot demonstrations to produce actions from visual and language input~\cite{brohan2023_rt2,kim2024_openvla,karamcheti2024,black2024_pi0,zheng2024tracevla,hung2025nora,xiao2025ava}.
5	NLP instruction tuning is well-characterized behaviorally~\cite{wei2022finetuned,ouyang2022training}, but the representational effects of VLA fine-tuning remain unexamined.
6	Fine-tuning operates in a low intrinsic dimension~\cite{aghajanyan2021intrinsic} and can distort pretrained features~\cite{kumar2022finetuning}; recent VLA-specific work proposes representation-preserving strategies~\cite{grover2025preserving,hancock2025actions}. %------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Cross-Architecture Analyses}
\label{sec:cross_arch_analyses}

Three analyses are applied to every available cell in the $3 \times 4$ matrix.

\paragraph{Action probes.}\looseness=-1
To quantify how much action-relevant structure is accessible at each layer, we train two-layer MLP probes~\cite{alain2017} to predict 7-DoF action vectors from frozen representations (architecture and training details in Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}).
We report probe $R^2$ as a measure of action decodability.
Higher $R^2$ indicates that actions are more accurately predictable from that representation under the probe; it should not be interpreted as evidence that the model causally uses that layer for action generation.
We define $\Delta R^2$ as the difference between the maximum layer-wise $R^2$ and the exit-layer $R^2$, and use $\Delta R^2 > 0.10$ as a descriptive threshold for substantial peak-to-exit reduction.
Train/test splits follow demonstration boundaries (demo-level splitting reduces $R^2$ from $0.7$--$0.9$ to $0.4$--$0.6$ vs.\ random splitting; Appendix~\ref{sec:delta_r2_threshold}).
95\% CIs are obtained via Monte Carlo cross-validation ($n = 1{,}000$ iterations) with demo-level resampling; the canonical peak layer is fixed from the full-data split to avoid winner's-curse bias.
Linear probes yield consistent patterns (Appendix~\ref{sec:linear_probe}).

\paragraph{L1 attention head profiling.}\looseness=-1
To determine whether attention heads preferentially route instruction information to the readout position, each L1 head is classified as instruction-dominant ($>50\%$ of readout-token attention to instruction tokens) or image-dominant, reported as $k/N$ heads (32 for MHA, 16 for GQA).
Sensitivity analysis at thresholds from $30\%$ to $70\%$ confirms ordering robustness (Appendix~\ref{sec:threshold_sensitivity}).

\paragraph{Counterfactual instruction perturbation.}\looseness=-1
To test whether the model's actions depend on instruction content, the instruction is replaced with four conditions: empty string, wrong task, shuffled tokens, and paraphrased.
We measure trained-model sensitivity via Cohen's $d$ on action MSE (OpenVLA, TraceVLA) or cosine distance (NORA); reference VLMs use cosine distance on hidden representations.
These metrics operate on different scales; cross-metric ratios are invalid (\S\ref{sec:cf_sensitivity}).

\enlargethispage{2\baselineskip}
\looseness=-1
OpenVLA additionally supports cross-instruction probes, representational similarity analysis (RSA)~\cite{kriegeskorte2008}, and external baselines (DINOv2~\cite{oquab2024_dinov2}, CLIP~\cite{radford2021_clip}); these single-architecture methods are detailed in Appendix~\ref{sec:openvla_methods_appendix}.
\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_rsa_perlayer_curve.pdf}
\vspace{-6pt}
\caption{Per-layer RSA ($\rho$) for trained/reference OpenVLA. Trained: inverted-U peaking at L12; reference: monotonic decline. Readout and image\_mean diverge after L12.}
\label{fig:rsa_perlayer}
\vspace{-6pt}
\end{figure}
Figure~\ref{fig:rsa_perlayer} previews this: per-layer geometric alignment ($\rho$) diverges between trained and reference models after L12, with trained readout tokens maintaining alignment ($\rho = 0.584$) while image-mean representations decay ($\rho = 0.422$), suggesting task-specific conditioning at the readout position.
